original_text: The resource-based view provides a useful framework for explaining why a pharmaceutical firm may acquire an innovative target instead of developing comparable assets internally. According to Barney (1991), sustained competitive advantage derives from resources that are valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and not readily substitutable. In the pharmaceutical context, such resources may include patented molecules, preclinical and clinical-stage pipeline assets, proprietary research platforms, clinical data, and highly specialised scientific expertise. These assets may have value in themselves by reason of their legal protection and the difficulty with which a competing company might replicate them through tacit knowledge: by acquiring them the existing company can leverage the target's inventive know-how along with its own manufacturing, regulatory, financial, and commercial capabilities, realizing value that the target may not have been able to achieve.

original_text: Building on the previous research, the knowledge-based view regards the company as an organisation which combines and coordinates specialised knowledge (Grant 1996). In pharmaceuticals, expertise is distributed across scientific teams, laboratories, therapeutic areas, and stages of development. Acquiring a firm that already possesses complementary knowledge may therefore be faster and less costly than reproducing that knowledge internally. However, it is important to note that ownership does not necessarily ensure successful knowledge transfer. Nelson and Winter’s (1982) evolutionary account suggests that knowledge is embedded in the organisational routines and experience through which it was developed, and such routines do not automatically transfer when control changes. Consequently, legal control of a target does not in itself guarantee that the acquirer will preserve or reproduce the processes supporting the target’s innovative capability.

Agency theory suggests that managers may pursue acquisitions to increase organisational size, visibility, or control even when the expected returns to shareholders are limited (Jensen, 1986). original_text: A further possible explanation for lower post-acquisition innovation is deliberate commercial choice rather than unsuccessful integration. Arrow’s (1962) replacement effect suggests that an incumbent has weaker incentives than an entrant to introduce an innovation that would cannibalise profits from existing products. Gilbert and Newbery (1982) develop a related pre-emption argument in which the incumbent invests in order to protect its market position. In pharmaceutical context the acquiring firm may perceive an acquired project as being worth less if the product it is targeting is closely related to a product the acquiring firm is currently selling or developing. It can be empirically illustrated at project level (Cunningham et al. 2021), that an acquired drug project is more likely to be discarded if it is related to other drug projects in the acquiring firm's R&D pipeline, particularly in low competitive segments, or when related patents have a long remaining time before expiation. original_text: Taken together, the theoretical perspectives reviewed above do not support a single prediction. The resource-based view, knowledge-based view, absorptive-capacity perspective, and complementary-assets theory explain how access to external knowledge may create value. In contrast, agency costs, disruption to organisational routines, weaker competitive pressure, and replacement incentives explain how value may be lost. Since these mechanisms may operate simultaneously and in opposite directions across innovation and financial performance, the two families of outcomes must first be estimated separately before their potential divergence can be examined.

original_text: The term innovation-driven acquisition is used in this thesis to refer to a completed transaction in which the target contributes a material and identifiable innovation asset to the combined firm and access to that asset constitutes a central observable purpose of the deal. These may be owned molecules; pipeline assets in pre-clinical and clinical development; patented entities/patent families; science/technology platforms; expert R&D staff; research data; discovery capabilities or clinical development expertise; diagnostic tools or other R&D-enabled technologies; research capabilities or scientific expertise, all defined based on tangible characteristics prior to completion rather than manager representations of intent. In the empirical design, candidate rationales such as expand offering / add products, access to resources, and forward or backward integration qualify only where the assets acquired are of the innovative types identified above.

Such a screen admits both false positives and false negatives. A false positive arises when a transaction motivated by financial or commercial considerations is assigned an innovation rationale—for example, where a mature asset base or a manufacturing or services facility is acquired without any meaningful pre-deal innovation asset. A false negative arises when a genuine pipeline, platform, or R&D capability is recorded under a rationale of scale, diversification, integration, or a purely transactional objective. Both forms of error were material in the transaction set used in this thesis and were reassigned using evidence available before completion.

original_text: A major difficulty in evaluating pharmaceutical innovation is that no single indicator provides a complete measure, and the interpretation of an acquisition may vary with the outcome selected. R&D expenditure is an input measure and does not indicate what the expenditure produces; a decline may reflect either weaker research effort or increased efficiency. Patent counts are a measure of coded output and treat inventions of vastly different importance the same. Forward citations can signal technological impact. The point estimates and the restricted wild-cluster bootstrap were consequently produced in Python using a hand-coded routine. Results were cross-checked across the linear fixed-effects, PPML, and IHS specifications, but independent replication in R has not yet been completed. Replication using the intended packages and unit-testing of the bootstrap routine are recorded as outstanding validation steps, so the custom bootstrap should not be described as fully validated.
